To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV-infected patients who have been treated with antiretrovirus for at least one year, and who have detectable viral loads, should be evaluated for resistance testing.
The use of resistance testing in the management of HIV-1-infected patients with antiretrovrial drug resistance can help guide the selection of appropriate antiretrovrials for these patients.
HIV-1 resistance testing and the use of resistance test-guided therapy can lead to significant virologic and immunologic benefits for patients with multidrug resistance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel class of antiretrovirus, the so-called antiretrovirals, and their use in the treatment of HIV-infected patients.
the development of new antiviral agents and the use of these agents to treat HIV-infected patients who have multidrug-resistant virus.
the development of new antiviral drugs and the design of new treatment regimens for the therapy of HIV-1 infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the treatment guidelines for antiretrovirus therapy in HIV-inflicted patients with multidrug resistant virus are not always applicable in practice.
the guidelines for treatment-experienced, antiretrovirus-resistant patients are evolving and should be individualized to the patient's needs.
the treatment of HIV-infected patients harboring multidrug-resistant HIV strains should be individualized and guided by clinical and virologic parameters.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of new agents with antiretrovirus resistance is an important part of the treatment of HIV infection.

the treatment of multidrug-resistant HIV is challenging, but with the application of the guidelines and the use of new antiretoviral agents, it is possible to achieve virologic suppression and clinical benefits in the majority of these patients.
antiretrovial therapy in HIV-inflicted patients with multi-drug resistant virus can be applied to the guidelines in practice.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of new antiretovirals, such as raltegravir, darunavir, and maraviroc, in the context of a multidrug-resistant viral strain, can lead to suppression of the viral load to <50 copies per milliliters, and that the use of resistance assays is critical to the selection of the appropriate antiretrovirals.
patients with multidrug resistance can achieve undetectable HIV-1 viral loads with the use of new agents and a multidisciplinary team of physicians.

the treatment of HIV-infected patients harboring multidrug-resistant virus can be successfully achieved by following a structured, stepwise approach that incorporates the use of resistance tests and the availability of newer, more effective antiretrovirals.
